 2005.  However, the Committee is not happy to note that every year the Ministry is furnishing same reasons such as land
 acquisition, removal of utilities, environmental/forest clearances, quarries etc. for delay in the execution of the
 projects.   The Government should be careful in handling court cases because if the cases are not handled properly, it
 would lead to further undue delay. The Committee, therefore, recommends that Ministry of Road Transport &
 Highways should evolve some mechanism to identify the traditional bottlenecks, which are causing delay and involve
 all the concerned agencies in the process of resolving all such hindrances.
 
5.         The Committee is happy to note that the improvement of the riding quality has led to great economic benefits for
 people living along the length of the roads. Roads are the key to the development of an economy. The Committee hopes
 that the revolution in the road sector will go a long way in promoting the economic development of the country and
 integrating remote regions with the mainstream economic activity by opening them to trade and investment.

(Recommendation at Para 30 and 32)
 
8.         The Committee in its 59
th Report on Demands for Grants 2002-03 of the Ministry of Road Transport and

 monitoring for utilisation of funds be ensured.  The Committee appreciates that there has been a major improvement in
 the rate of utilisation of Central Road Fund by the States/UTs as compared to the earlier years.  The Committee notes
 with satisfaction that the funds allocated for maintenance and development of National Highways to the States/UTs was
 expected to be fully utilised by them during 2002-03.  The Committee recommends that there should be no let up in the

9.         The Committee is of the view that since the allocation out of the CRF for the State Highways is done by the
 Ministry of Road Transport and Highways, it becomes the responsibility of the Ministry to ensure proper utilisation of
 the funds.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways should develop

 purpose only.

MAINTENANCE AND REPAIRS OF NATIONAL HIGHWAYS
(Recommendation at Para 37)
           
12.       The Committee is of the view that if the roads are not well maintained, it would certainly have an adverse impact
 on the aspect of road safety and also the investments made in the construction of the roads go waste.  The Committee is
 constrained to note that the financial resources made available to the Ministry under Maintenance & Repairs head (Non-
Plan) have been only 40% of the requirement projected by the Ministry of Road Transport & Highways.  The Committee
 understands that there is available capacity in the Ministry of Road Transport & Highways to undertake more works for
 maintenance and repair of roads.  The Committee recommends that the Ministry of Road Transport & Highways should
 utilise funds available for the purpose in the initial few months of the financial year so that the Ministry can
 emphatically impress upon the Government for higher allocation of funds for maintenance and repair of roads at the RE
 stage.  The Committee also recommends that higher allocations be made in the coming years to Ministry of Road
 Transport & Highways for maintenance and repair of roads.
 
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
 
13.       The Ministry is taking necessary steps for sanction of the estimates for maintenance of National Highways
 (Periodic Renewal/Special Repair) in the beginning of the financial year so that the allocated fund can be utilized early
 and additional funds for maintenance can be sought for at the “Revised Estimate” stage.
 
FURTHER RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION OF THE COMMITTEE
 
14.       The Committee notes the reply of the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways.  The Committee would like to
 be informed of the sanctions made for maintenance of National Highways (Periodical Renewal/Special Repair) by the
 Ministry of Road Transport and Highways upto September 2003 and additional funds sought by the Ministry at the RE
 stage.
 
FEE/TOLL TAX ON BRIDGES AND NATIONAL HIGHWAYS
(Recommendation at Para 42)
 
15.       The Committee is not convinced with the reasons advanced by the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways for
 collecting toll on roads and bridges in perpetuity.  The Committee feels that the Government is not justified in
 burdening the common people with the development as well as the maintenance of the roads in the country.  The
 Committee had also commented upon this matter in its 43
rd Report on Demands for Grants 2000-2001 of the then
 Ministry of Surface Transport.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that once the cost of construction of a
 road/bridge plus interest is recovered, the collection of toll should be stopped.   The Committee also feels that there
 exists a need for the rationalisation of the toll tax being charged on the National Highways.  The Committee
 recommends that persons travelling on smaller stretches of the National Highways where toll is being collected should
 be charged a lower amount than the persons using the entire length of that National Highway.
 
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
 
16.       The policy of levying users fee on roads and bridges was adopted to defray the cost of construction and
 maintenance due to budgetary resource constraints.  Levying of users fee is based on the principle of upgradation of the
 facility resulting in reduced vehicle cost, reduced travel time and enhanced safety.  Development and maintenance of
 highways being a continuous process it was decided to levy fee in perpetuity to have constant flow of fund.  The total
 amount of bridge fee as collected is spent in the State from which it is levied.  Thus, this fee is utilized for improving the
 National Highways in the State itself.  In view of the above the Committee may kindly reconsider their

 recommendations.
 
17.       The Users’ fee on National Highways is being collected on “Open Tolling” system.  It means the tolled portion is
 not access controlled.  The users’ fee is charged on the basis of the distance between two tollgates.  The location of
 tollgates is decided on the basis of convenience of traffic, location of major access roads, travel pattern and cost of toll
 collection.  In the ‘Open Tolling’ system it is difficult to implement differential rates of users’ fees.  The users’ fee on
 the basis of distance traveled can be charged in the “Closed Tolling” system where the accesses are controlled.  This is
 not yet feasible in the country.  In view of the above the Committee may kindly reconsider their recommendation.
 
FURTHER RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION OF THE COMMITTEE
 
18.       The Committee does not agree with the reply of the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways for collecting toll
 on roads and bridges in perpetuity.  Development and maintenance of highways is no doubt a continuous process but the
 Government cannot absolve itself of its responsibilities in this respect by shifting its entire burden on the common
 people.  In order to help the Government overcome the budgetary financial constraints, the toll should be collected till
 such time the cost of construction of a road/bridge plus interest is recovered.  The Committee, therefore, reiterates its
 earlier recommendation that once the cost of construction of a road/bridge plus interest is recovered, the collection of
 toll should be stopped.
 
19.       The Committee  takes note of the reply of the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways with respect to the
 Committee’s recommendation regarding charging of users fee on the basis of distance travelled.  The Committee feels
 that in the present system of tolling, persons traveling in smaller stretches of the National Highways where toll is being
 collected are in a disadvantageous position.  Such a situation cannot be allowed to go on forever.  The Committee,
 therefore, recommends that the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways should initiate the steps to develop a system
 whereby the users’ fee could be charged on the basis of the distance travelled.
 
PORT CONNECTIVITY PROJECTS
(Recommendation at Para 46)
 
20.       The Committee feels that connectivity of the ports to the National Highways is of great importance from the
 point of view of commercial and industrial production.  The Committee is surprised to note that Mumbai Port Trust has
 not been included in the port connectivity projects.  The Committee has been informed that there is no proper road link
 to Mumbai Port and the only available road route to the port is in a poor condition.  The Committee, therefore,
 recommends that the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways should also include the Mumbai Port in their port
 connectivity project.   For this purpose, they can also approach the Mumbai Port Trust for their assistance in the project.
 
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
 
21.       Major ports are to be connected under Port Connectivity Programme as mandated to NHAI.  Feasibility for
 connection of Mumbai Port was examined and it was observed that there was hardly any scope for the improvement of
 approach road to the Mumbai Port as it passed through heavily populated area of Mumbai city.  The only option was to
 construct a new elevated road which would have to pass through long stretch of salt pans and marshy land.  Mumbai
 Port Trust also advised that unless the matters were sorted out, further detailed study should not be carried out.  In view
 of the fact that construction of such a long section of elevated road will be extremely costly and such a huge investment
 might not justify the benefit which will accrue and this would also involve a large extent of land acquisition and
 environmental issued, it was decided not to take up this stretch at this stage.  However, on the advise of the Standing
 Committee the matter is being taken up once again with the Mumbai Port Trust.
 
FURTHER RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION OF THE COMMITTEE

 by the Government besides highway design to check the road accidents are as under:

28.            Enforcement of provisions of Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 and Central Motor Vehicles Rules, 1989 for improved
 road safety is entirely the responsibility of State Government.
 
29.            Upgradation of technology and concomitant norms for safety related automotive components is a continuous
 ongoing exercise.  The automotive standards/norms are gradually being harmonized with ECE specifications.  These
 norms are being constantly upgraded and notified on the basis of recommendations of the Central Motor Vehicles Rules
 Technical Standing Committee.
 
30.       As a result of efforts made by Central/State Governments, accident rate per 1000 vehicles has come down from
 10.98 in 1996 to 8.09 (provisional) in 2000. 
 
FURTHER RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION OF THE COMMITTEE
 
31.       The Committee notes the reply of the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways.  The Committee further notes
 that accident rate per 1000 vehicles has come down from 10.98 in 1996 to 8.09 in 2000 and hopes that that steps taken
 by Ministry of Road Transport and Highways would result in further decrease in the accident rate of vehicles which is
 still very high.
 
ROAD TRANSPORT
(Recommendation at Para 58)
 
32.       The Committee feels that with the development and improvement in riding quality of the roads, danger to the
 lives of the villagers and cattle has also increased on those roads.  Inspite of the construction of underpasses at the
 traditional crossing points, the incidents of accidents on such roads has been rising.  The Committee, therefore,
 recommends that while undertaking the development of the roads, the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways should
 make some extra efforts and, if necessary, construct underpasses and over-bridges, taking into account the population
 and the requirement of the users of that area so that accidents can be avoided and there is no loss of lives.  Systematic
 survey for assessment of users convenience should also be conducted in this regard.  
 
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
 
33.       The four/six laning of National Highway Project considers the provision of under passes and over bridges at
 congested and populated areas for the safety of the habitants in the adjoining areas.  The four/six laning project is
 prepared on the basis of detailed engineering.  The requirement of under passes/over bridges is assessed on the basis of
 number of population and vehicles.  Location of these structures is decided on the basis of engineering requirements and
 also the most preferred point(s) of crossing.  These factors are considered while preparation of the detailed project report
 of the improvement works.  Hence it would be seen that the recommendation of the Hon’ble Standing Committee is
 being followed.

PROBLEM OF OVERLOADING
(Recommendation at Para 65)
 
35.       The Committee is of the view that the problem of overloading of vehicles has been growing steadily inspite of
 the measures adopted by the Ministry of Road Transport & Highways.  The Committee feels that overloading of
 vehicles has not only been causing early destruction of several road stretches but also resulting in accidents leading to
 loss of life and property.  The Committee is constrained to note that certain state governments have been regularising
 overloading for financial gains.  The Committee appreciates the States of Karnataka, West Bengal, Meghalaya, Uttar
 Pradesh, Tripura and Gujarat for offering tax rebate to popularise the use of multi axle vehicles.  The Committee
 recommends that the Ministry of Road Transport & Highways should further take up the matter with the concerned state
 governments so as to check the problem of overloading. Also the legislation proposed for this purpose should be
 introduced at the earliest.  The Committee also reiterates the recommendations made in its 59
th Report that the Ministry
 of Road Transport & Highways should come up with publicity efforts, on large scale, addressing to the truck drivers and
 the agencies engaged in transportation business, including general public.  Themes dealing with dangers of overloading
 should form an important part of the publicity campaigns undertaken in this regard.  Also awareness campaigns should
 be launched including advertisements in print/electronic media. 
 
 
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
 
36.       Motor Vehicles Act has strict provisions for tackling overloading.  Enforcement of these provisions is
 responsibility of the State Government. The Transport Development Council in its 30th meeting on 16.1.2003 had
 discussed this matter and it was agreed that:
 
a)      Strict enforcement of the provisions relating to overloading under the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 and Central
 Motor Vehicles Rules, 1989.
b)      The State Governments are not to issue special cards/passes which legalize overloading.
c)      The decision of the 28th meeting of TDC held on 10.10.1998 for states to give a 25% tax rebate to popularize
 use of multi axle vehicles, which has been implemented so far by a few States like Karnataka, West Bengal,
 Meghalaya, Uttar Pradesh, Tripura and Gujarat, may be carried out by other States also.
d)         Keeping in view a number of court cases, the registering authority shall ensure that the vehicles are registered
 only as per the load ceilings notified and in case erroneously a higher load rating has been incorporated, then
 the same shall be got rectified.
e)      Non-renewal of registration and denial of permit to habitual offenders of overloading.
 
Subsequently, this matter has been continuously taken up with the State Governments.
 
37.            MOS(RT&H) and Secretary(RT&H) have written a number of letters to the State Governments pointing out
 that the practice of issuing special cards/ token, which have the effect of legitimizing overloading should be stopped and
 that the Central Government would be constrained to stop the releases from the Central Road Fund to the State
 Governments.   MOS(RT&H) has written to Chief Minister of Madhya Pradesh on 3rd April, 2003 and subsequently to
 Chief Ministers of Chhattisgarh, Gujarat, Uttar Pradesh, Rajasthan, Orissa and Haryana on 19.4.2003.  Similarly,
 Secretary(RT&H) has written to all states on 4th March, 2003.  Subsequently, Secretary(RT&H) has again addressed the
 Chief Secretaries of several states, namely Madhya Pradesh & Rajasthan(21.3.2003), Uttar Pradesh, Orissa & Gujarat
 (7.4.2003) and again to Rajasthan, Orissa & Uttar Pradesh (17.4.2003) and Haryana and Uttar Pradesh (on 20.4.2003
 and 29.4.2003 respectively).
 
38.       The Committee’s suggestion regarding making appropriate amendments in the Motor Vehicles Act to tackle
 overloading in an effective manner has been noted.    In fact, a proposal recommending amendment of sec. 194 & 200 of
 the M.V. Act removing the powers of State Governments to compound the offence of overloading has been sent to M/o
 Law for vetting as a part of the comprehensive proposal for amendment of M.V. Act.

THE APPROACH IN THE 10
TH PLAN AND ANALYSIS OF THE ANNUAL PLAN 2003-04 (Recommendation
 at para 10)
 
5.         The Committee observes that for the 10 th plan an amount of Rs.1720 crores inclusive of Rs.180 crores for
 Capital Component has been allocated for plan expenditure of the Department of Culture.  Out of which only Rs.250
 crores had been allocated during the first year of the 10
th Plan i.e. 2002-03 and an amount of Rs.250 crores has been
 allocated in B.E. 2003-04 as the plan outlay of Department of Culture against the projected requirement of Rs.399
 crores.  The Committee is constrained to note that the share of the Department in terms of total plan allocation of the
 Government is only 0.2 per cent, which is abysmally low.  The Committee finds that the plan outlay approved by the
 Government of India is on lower side in comparison to the amount proposed by the Department of Culture for 2003-
04.  The Committee feels that the Government has not paid adequate attention to this Sector. The Committee
 disapproves the low pace of allocation of outlay to the Department of Culture out of the total approved allocation
 outlay, i.e. of Rs.1720 crores for the plan expenditure to be made during the 10
th five-year plan.  The Committee feels
 that any reduction in the outlay would have serious implications in the development activities of the Department.  The
 Committee, recommends that in future the Department should be allocated with more funds in order to enable them to
 fulfill the targets and the Government of India should address the financial requirements of the Department of Culture
 more realistically and allocate the amount more judiciously while sanctioning the plan outlay for the remaining periods
 of the 10th Plan.

6.         The matter has been taken up with the Planning Commission and their comments are awaited.

 Planning Commission for allocation of more funds to Department for the remaining period of the 10
th Plan.

(Recommendation at para 14)

 capital works.  The amount earmarked for capital works is also reflected in the Demands for Grants of Ministry of
 Urban Development.  The money is spent by CPWD on the projects of Department of Culture.  The Committee took
 serious note of the reduction of the amount at Revised Estimate stage by the Ministry of Urban development
 unilaterally that too without taking them into confidence. The Committee also notes that the capital works outlay during
 IX Plan was Rs.112 crores and CPWD could spend only Rs.59.29 crores i.e. 52.94 per cent of the total allocation,
 where as projects of Department of Culture suffered severe financial crunch.  Therefore, the Committee recommends
 that this anomalous practice should be stopped at once.  The Committee further recommends that the amount for the
 capital works should be allocated in the Demands for Grants of the Department of Culture and placed at the disposal of
 Department of Culture instead of Ministry of Urban Development in order to ensure better implementation control and
 monitoring of projects.

ARCHAEOLOGICAL SURVEY OF INDIA
(Recommendation at paras 21, 24& 29)
 
11.       The Committee is happy to note that the Ministry of Finance has released 75 per cent of the revenue collected
 through entry fee to the Department of Culture at the revised estimate stage during 2002-03 for conservation and
 maintenance of monuments.  The Committee feels that execution of conservation and preservation works need an
 excellent expertise and timely funding of projects.  But with its meager resource, it was difficult for the ASI to protect
 and maintain all the 3616 monuments/sites.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that 100 per cent of the revenue
 collected from admission fees should be released to ASI for stepping up the activities and to augment resources of ASI
 besides coordinated efforts should be taken by the ASI to bring more monuments under central protection and also
 raising the number of monuments for ticketing purpose to generate more revenue.
 
12.       The Committee is happy to note that three new Circles in the States of Uttranchal, Jharkhand and Chattisgarh
 have been created under ASI and will be operational from April 2003, which will result in intensive preservation and
 maintenance of monuments in more sites.  The Committee is not satisfied with the efforts of the Department of Culture
 with regard to filling up of vacant posts in ASI and recommends that ASI should fill up these vacant posts within a
 definite time frame, so that execution of Conservation, Preservation and Developmental work of monuments do not
 suffer for want of shortage of manpower.  
                                                                                                                  
13.       The Committee notes that ASI has drawn long term programme to protect all 3616 monuments/sites of national
 importance.  These monuments have also been classified into three categories viz. Group A, B and C.  The Committee
 also notes that Group A consists of 16 monuments inscribed in the World Heritage list and 11 monuments have been
 proposed to the UNESCO for inclusion in the list of World Heritage Sites.  The Committee recommends that
 Department of Culture should identify at least one monument/site in each State for inclusion in the list of World
 Heritage Sites of UNESCO and coordinated efforts should be made for integrated infrastructure development
 conservation/preservation of these monuments sites with encompassing facilities for tourists, so as to give a major fillip
 to cultural tourism in the country as well as attracting overseas visitors.

14.       Upto 2001, 3606 monuments were under protection.   As on date, 3622 monuments have been protected and
 included in the national list of centrally protected monuments.  This is an on going process considering the historical,
 archaeological and aesthetic importance of monuments.
 
15.       All the three newly created Circles at Raipur, Ranchi and Dehradun have become fully functional with adequate
 manpower, budget and financial powers.  As regards filling up the vacant posts, continuous efforts are being made to
 fill them up.
 
16.       The 11 sites under the present tentative list of UNESCO covers 9 States of the country, namely, Andhra Pradesh,
 Bihar, Delhi, Gujarat, Karnataka, Kerala, Madhya Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh and West Bengal.  The Prehistoric Rock
 Shelters and Caves with paintings at Bhimbetka, Madhya Pradesh has been nominated for inscription on the World
 Heritage List for 2003.  At present, there is an embargo imposed by UNESCO under which only one site per country
 can be nominated in a year.  Integrated development of the sites in a befitting manner to attract more tourists is the
 present priority of the Department of Culture.

AIR INDIA LIMITED
(Recommendation at Para 13)
 
5.         The Committee is not satisfied with the reply furnished by the Ministry of Civil Aviation for non-utilisation of
 plan outlay prescribed for non-aircraft projects of Air India.  The Committee feels that there is lack of proper planning
 in Air India, as a result of which the Company fails to make financial provision for the schemes envisaged by it.  The
 Committee, therefore, recommends that Air India should make a realistic assessment of its requirements and the ability
 of the company to make financial provisions for the same.
 
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
 
6.         Air India has noted the recommendations of the Committee.  AI had provided Rs.150 crores as capital
 expenditure outlay towards non-aircraft project for the year 2002-03.  Considering the economy measures, capital
 expenditure was committed at Rs.67 crores without compromising on levels of service and safety.  The unspent amount
 has been carried forward to 2003-04 under Continuing Schemes of the Capital Budget of 2003-04.
 
FURTHER RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION OF THE COMMITTEE
 
7.         The Committee notes the reply of the Ministry of Civil Aviation.
 
INDIAN AIRLINES LIMITED
(Recommendation at Para 21)
 
8.         The Committee is not convinced with the reply furnished by the Ministry of Civil Aviation for not being able to
 correctly estimate the loss of Indian Airlines during 2002-2003.  The Committee notes that the estimated loss of Indian
 Airlines was more than four times of the loss projected by the Company, which clearly indicates the inability of the
 Company to make a correct assessment of its financial performance.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that
 Indian Airlines should evolve a mechanism whereby they could make a realistic assessment of its financial performance
 keeping in view the prevalent market scenario and economic conditions.
 
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
 
9.         The recommendation has been noted for compliance.
 
FURTHER RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION OF THE COMMITTEE
 
10.       The Committee notes the reply of the Ministry of Civil Aviation, However, the Committee would like to know
 the steps taken by the Ministry of Civil Aviation/Indian Airlines to make a realistic assessment of its financial
 performance.
 
EXPANSION OF FLEET BY INDIAN AIRLINES/AIR INDIA
(Recommendation at Para 31)
 
11.       The Committee notes that the fleet expansion programme of Indian Airlines has been held up for the last one
 year since the Company was rostered for disinvestment.  The Committee is aware that Shipping Corporation of India,
 Mumbai, a Public Sector Undertaking under the Ministry of Shipping, which is also proposed to be disinvested, has
 placed orders for acquiring 9 vessels in October 2002.  The Committee fails to understand as to why there are two sets
 of rules for the Public Sector Undertakings of the Government of India.  On the one hand Indian Airlines is not being

 since it has to compete with other private airlines which have new and better aircraft and are, therefore, able to
 encroach upon the market share of Indian Airlines.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that all necessary
 clearances/approvals for fleet expansion by Indian Airlines and Air India should be granted at the earliest.  The
 induction of new aircraft and the optimum use of the existing fleet by Indian Airlines would go a long way in
 increasing its market share, efficiency and profitability.

NON-UTILISATION OF ILS CAT-IIIA AT IGI AIRPORT, DELHI.
(Recommendation at Para 44)
 
20.       The Committee is constrained to note that the progress made with regard to the training of pilots for effectively
 utilizing the ILS CAT IIIA system is highly unsatisfactory in respect of both Indian Airlines and Air India.  The
 Committee wishes to express its anguish over the fact that after making huge investment for the installation of the
 modern technologies at the airports, the instruments remain lying idle for want of trained personnel.  Also, the
 operational capability of the system cannot be judged without effectively utilizing the system.  The Committee feels
 that the pilots should have been given training simultaneously at the time of the installation of the system.  The
 Committee hopes that the system does not become obsolete by the time our national carriers have trained personnel to
 utilize the system.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry of Civil Aviation should take some
 immediate steps so that the training of the pilots can be completed in a time bound manner and the modernized system
 installed at the India Gandhi International Airport could be put to optimum use, thereby reducing the hardships of the
 passengers during the foggy periods.

30.       The Committee is of the opinion that the dimensions of aviation security have changed significantly during the
 last few years.  The Committee feels that in view of the huge costs incurred towards the deployment of CISF at the
 airports, there is a need to have a re-look into the proposal.  The Committee recommends that the Ministry of Civil
 Aviation should explore the possibility of setting up of a dedicated Civil Aviation Security Force, under the
 administrative control of the Ministry.  This would not only be beneficial from the point of view of administrative
 control but also result in employment generation in the various parts of the country.
 
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
 
31.       The issue regarding creation of a separate Aviation Security Force was under active consideration of the
 Government till December 1999.  In the wake of hijacking of Indian Airlines flight IC-814 on 24
th December, 1999, the
 Government of India decided to induct CISF at all operational airports in the country, after imparting necessary
 training.  CISF has already been deployed at 46 operational airports of the country and is being deployed at the
 remaining operational airports in a phased manner.
 
32.       Since CISF has been functioning quite satisfactorily and have gained sufficient experience in the field of
 aviation security; no separate civil aviation security force is proposed to be set up.
 
33.       While it is true that expenditure is being incurred on CISF it appears that the creation of a separate AVSEC force
 will be more expensive as in that case AAI will become totally responsible for the upkeep of the force.
 
FURTHER RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION OF THE COMMITTEE
           
34.       The Committee notes the reply of Ministry of Civil Aviation.  However, the Committee feels that the question of
 cost incurred has to be studied as compared to the cost, which was earlier being incurred by the deployment of state

 cost as well as impact of the present salary and perquisites and their modalities.

39.       Fuel plays a crucial role in the cost structure and profitability of any airline.  The Committee is of the view that
 the high cost of ATF for domestic air transport increases the cost of operation and makes it unviable even in areas
 where it has comparative advantage over other modes of transport.  The Committee appreciates the initiative taken by
 the State Government of Andhra Pradesh in reducing the rate of sales tax on ATF to 4 percent.  The Committee hopes
 that this step of the Government of Andhra Pradesh would encourage the other State Governments to follow suit.  The
 Committee recommends that Ministry of Civil Aviation should impress upon the State Governments to come forward
 and reduce the sales tax on ATF to the minimum level, preferably 4 per cent.

 the State Governments with respect to the requirements of air connectivity etc. for their states and try to evolve a
 solution whereby decision on all these problems could be taken as a package deal.

 have also met Chief Ministers/Chief Secretaries of State Governments in this regard.  The difficulties being faced in
 providing air connectivity to various locations due to commercial unviability of operations on account of high ATF
 prices have also been impressed upon the State Governments.

DEVELOPMENT AND MAINTENANCE OF AIRPORTS BY AIRPORTS AUTHORITY OF INDIA.
(Recommendation at Para 63)
 
43.       The Committee is not convinced with the replies furnished by the Ministry of Civil Aviation with regard to
 making investments at certain airports while withdrawing the flights to/from such stations.  The Committee is of the
 view that there is no coordination between the various executive wings of the Ministry of Civil Aviation.  The
 Committee feels that while improving the infrastructure at the airports, there is a simultaneous need to provide air
 connectivity to such places, in absence of which the investments made forwards development of airports go waste.  The
 Committee also feels that Airports Authority of India is not taking due care of its assets as is evident from the incident
 regarding illegal sale of the land of the Airports Authority of India.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that there
 should be better coordination between the various agencies of the Ministry of Civil Aviation.  The Committee also
 recommends that Airports Authority of India should evolve some mechanism to take better care of vast lands at its
 disposal.
 
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
 
44.       Airports Authority of India has evolved major initiatives for protecting its land resources from encroachment and
 illegal occupation. Apart from identification of the lands belonging to AAI and classification of the land records in a
 scientific way, the Land management Department has been strengthened by posting senior officers at the international
 airports as well as the Regional Headquarters. This Department has completed identification of the land holdings
 including land encroachment at all the airports. The process of building of the land records is in progress by employing
 specialized personnel like Tehsildars, Patwaris, Revenue Officers, at respective unit level. AAI has also identified a
 total of 682 acres of land encroached at 20 airports and action has been initiated to remove these encroachments by
 taking up the matter with the State Governments. Action has also been initiated to protect airport lands from further
 encroachments and to provide security by construction of boundary walls, barbed wire fencing along the perimeter
 road, deploying Security Guards, etc. Such investments are unavoidable to protect the assets of AAI. Investments are
 also made for maintaining the facilities in operational status at operational airports irrespective of whether scheduled
 flights take place or not. Some airports are maintained in operational condition since casual operations take place at
 these airports. In addition, AAI also undertakes periodical maintenance of all operational airports, which include

 in the matter of development of Nagpur Airport as an International Multi Model Hub as soon as decision in this regard
 is taken by the Government.
 
FURTHER RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION OF THE COMMITTEE
 
48.       The Committee notes the reply of the Ministry of Civil Aviation and recommends that final decision in the
 matter be communicated to the Committee soon.
 
DEVELOPMENT AND MAINTENANCE OF AIRPORTS BY AIRPORTS AUTHORITY OF INDIA.
(Recommendation at Para 69)
 
49.       The Committee feels that in the present day context, there is a need of upgradation of small airfields located in
 various states such as Cooch Behar and Balaghat in West Bengal and Ajmer in Rajasthan.  The Committee also
 understands that many State Governments are willing to contribute to the development of such airports.  The
 Committee recommends that the Ministry of Civil Aviation should take initiative in this regard and get the opinion of
 the State Governments as to whether such airfields can be run with their contribution, in the respective States.  The
 Committee feels that the development of such airfields will certainly pave the way for providing inter-state air
 connectivity in those states.
 
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
 
50.       In 1989, Airports Authority of India had written to various State Governments to take over the non-operational
 airports in the States for upkeep and maintenance and also for use by the respective State Governments. None of the
 State Governments excepting the Government of Maharashtra had responded to our request for takeover and
 maintenance of the airports. Only the Government of Maharashtra has responded and two airports namely Sholapur and
 Kohlapur have been leased out to the State Government of Maharashtra for a period of 15 years for upgradation,
 maintenance and upkeep of the facilities. None of the other State Governments have responded to the request of AAI
 for taking over these non-operational airports.

Balurghat and Cooch Behar airports in West Bengal
 
51.       The airstrip at Balurghat and Cooch Behar in West Bengal are suitable for operation of 20-seater type of aircraft.
 Both the aerodromes need extensive maintenance and renovation works before commencement of any schedule
 operation. There is no scope for expansion of these aerodromes. There is no operation through these aerodromes for
 more than 15 years. No request has been received from the State Government regarding taking over of these airports for
 development purpose. There is no commitment or request from any schedule airline for reactivation of these two
 aerodromes. Therefore, AAI has no plan to develop these aerodromes in the West Bengal.
 
Ajmer
 
52.       At the request of State Government of Rajasthan, AAI has examined a site near Kayar village at Ajmer about its
 suitability for construction of an airport. State Government was requested to acquire the land measuring about 1200
 acres and take necessary statutory clearances from the Central Government before development work is taken up. AAI
 has no plan to construct an airport at Ajmer, as this airport will be a loss-making airport. 
 
FURTHER RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION OF THE COMMITTEE
 
53.       The Committee notes the reply of the Ministry of Civil Aviation.
 
SCHEDULE OF VARIOUS DOMESTIC AIRLINES
(Recommendation at Para 74)
 
54.       Although Ministry of Civil Aviation have stated in their reply that the process of approval of the schedules has to
 be such as to avoid allegations of lack of transparency and motivated fixation of timings, the Committee is constrained
 to note that prime  timings are being given to the private airlines and Indian Airlines operates its flights at odd hours
 which not only results in inconvenience to the passengers but also most of the passengers load is diverted towards
 private airlines.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that this issue should be seriously looked into and flight
 timings of Indian Airlines flights should be rescheduled for better utilization of its seat capacity.  The Committee also
 recommends that there should be coordination between the Indian Airlines and the private airlines at the time of
 finalisation of their schedule so that there is a staggering of the multiple flights existing at peak hours, which would
 result in improved air services to the passengers during the non-peak hours also.
 
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
 
55.       Most of the flights of Indian Airlines have the historical time slots based
on the market requirements experienced over a period of time.  The private
airlines have been scheduling flights close to Indian Airlines timings.
 
56.       The schedule (flight timings) are the primary product attribute in the airline business.  The inherent nature of the
 domestic market is such that demand  on most domestic routes tends to be concentrated around peak periods, and all
 airlines therefore, tend to fix their timings during this peak period in order to be able to attract the maximum number of
 passengers.  For this reason, flight timings of airlines tend to be close to each other.  For example, on major metros,
 morning and evening time slots are preferred by all airlines.
 
57.       Further, flight timings depend on a number of factors like availability of aircraft crew and other resources,
 airfield characteristics etc. Indian Airlines accordingly schedules its flights taking into these factors and the deployment
 guidelines issued by DGCA.
 
FURTHER RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION OF THE COMMITTEE
 
58.       The Committee notes that the present reply of the Ministry of Civil Aviation, i.e., "private airlines have been

 scheduling flights close to Indian Airlines timings" is contradictory to their earlier reply. The Ministry had earlier
 submitted that the flight schedules are finally approved by DGCA.  The Committee takes strong exception to the
 present reply submitted by the Ministry, which does not fully reflect the facts.  The Committee, therefore, recommends
 that Government should identify more realistic & viable routes for Indian Airlines and reschedule its flight timings for
 better utilisation of seat capacity in comparison to the private airlines. 
 
59.       The Committee also notes the reply with respect to the recommendation of the Committee regarding staggering
 of the multiple flights existing at peak hours. However, the Committee reiterates its recommendation and feels that
 staggering of the multiple flights would not only offer better choice to the passengers, but would also result in
 decongestion of the airports at both arrival and departure lounges. This would also help our national carriers to increase
 their revenue and minimize their losses.

9.         According to the 10 th Five-Year Plan, the civil aviation sector has to play an important role in India's economy.  This
 sector will play a more significant role in integrating the Indian economy with the rest of the world.  But the importance
 attached to the civil aviation sector is not reflected in the outlays approved for the first two years of the 10 th Plan period of the
 Ministry of Civil Aviation.   The annual plan outlay of the Ministry of Civil Aviation was reduced from Rs.1779.18 crore for
 the year 2003-2004 to Rs.1469.77 crore at RE stage.  The reduction had been both in the Internal and Extra Budgetary
 Resources (IEBR) component as well as the Gross Budgetary support.  Now an outlay of Rs.1620.98 crore has been approved
 for the year 2004-05.  Thus an amount of Rs.3090.75 crore has been approved for the first two years of the 10 th Plan period. 
 Hence, only 23.9 per cent of the allocation has been approved for the first two years of the 10 th Plan which is fairly short of the
 proportionate 40% allocation which becomes due for this period.  The Committee recommends that keeping in view the
 importance of the civil aviation sector in the contemporary era, the Government should increase the outlay of Ministry of Civil
 Aviation and, if need be, supplement the allocation by substantially increasing the Gross Budgetary Support to the Ministry.

 Only in January 2004, Air India   submitted a Project Report for acquisition of 10 A340-300 aircraft and 18 B737-800 aircraft
 to the Ministry of Civil Aviation.  The proposal is under examination of Government in accordance with the investment
 procedures for PSUs.  As regards Indian Airlines, the Committee was informed that a proposal was received from Indian
 Airlines for acquisition of 43 aircraft comprising A319, A320, and A321 from M/s. Airbus Industries during the period 2003-04
 to 2007-08. The tentative cost of the project approximately is Rs. 10,089 crore. The new aircraft were envisaged to replace the
 entire fleet of A-300 and     B-737 aircraft, in a phased manner. The final decision on the proposal could not be taken as Indian
 Airlines was on disinvestment list till April 2003. 
 
20.        The Committee has, during the last 3-4 years, repeatedly emphasized in its reports on Demands for Grants of the
 Ministry of Civil Aviation that there is a need for expansion of the fleet and replacement of the aged aircraft of Indian Airlines. 
 The Committee feels that the fleet acquisition programme of the national carriers i.e., both Indian Airlines and Air India, has
 been ignored for long, as a result of which the two companies have suffered both financially as well as commercially.    Delay
 in fleet acquisition forced Air India to sell the bilateral agreements to foreign airlines as a result of which Air India lost its
 market share which has gone down to 20% which was at one time at 30%. The Committee is of the opinion that atmosphere of
 uncertainty prevailed due to confusion in the Government.   The fleet acquisition programme of the two airlines could not
 materialize due to the prevailing indecisiveness with regard to the management of the companies.  Firstly, the two companies
 were placed in the list of PSUs proposed to be disinvested and then later, their names were deleted from the said list.  The
 Committee noted the fact that now the Government has decided not to go in for their disinvestment.  The Committee is of the
 view that the fleet acquisition was the basic requirement for running the two companies commercially.  The Committee,
 therefore, recommends that the proposals of the Indian Airlines and Air India for acquisition of aircraft should be approved
 without any further delay.  In this regard, the Committee would also like to refer to its recommendations contained in 58
th
 Report (Para 39) and 69 th Report (Para 31) of this Committee on the Demands for Grants regarding fleet acquisition by Air
 India and Indian Airlines.

HIGH COST OF AIR TURBINE FUEL (ATF)
 
23.        During the course of the evidence of the representatives of Ministry of Civil Aviation, the Committee was informed that
 the domestic air transport industry in India has been facing serious problems due to high cost of operations. One of the major
 reasons for this is the heavy cost of Air Turbine Fuel (ATF).  Even though the pricing of ATF is now on import parity basis, the
 rates applicable for domestic operations continue to be significantly higher than that of international operations.  The cost of
 ATF goes up even further due to high rates of sales tax levied by the State Governments/Union Territory administration varying
 from 20 per cent to 36 per cent which affects the viability of domestic airline operations. 
 
24.        It was brought to the notice of the Committee that in March 2000, the cost of ATF was Rs.15,000 per Kl. and in August
 2004, the cost of ATF has gone upto Rs.27,000 per Kl.  Besides Central Excise, Base Price and Sales Tax on ATF is also paid. 
 It was also brought out that in developing countries and even in neighbouring South-East Asian countries and Gulf, the aviation
 fuel accounts for nearly 15% of the operating cost whereas in our country, it was costing nearly 31% of the total operating cost. 
 The representatives of Air India submitted that as per an international agreement, aircraft belonging to a foreign airline
 operating international service to, from and through India are exempted from payment of all custom duties, local duties, taxes,
 etc. on ATF and other items.  However, similar concessions were not available to Air India in India.  Hence, they were at a
 disadvantageous position vis-a-vis other foreign airlines operating to/from India. 
25.        The Committee had also taken up the issue relating to rationalization of sales tax on ATF in its 69
th Report on Demands
 for Grants 2003-04 of the Ministry of Civil Aviation and had recommended that  Ministry of Civil Aviation should impress
 upon the State Governments to reduce the sales tax on ATF to the minimum level.  In response the Committee was informed
 that the then Minister of Civil Aviation had written to the Chief Minister of State Governments requesting to consider
 appropriate reduction in the rate of sales tax on ATF in their respective states.  However, no favourable response has been
 received.  Some state governments have indicated that they can consider reduction provided they are compensated by the
 Central Government for the loss.
 
26.        The Committee feels that high cost of ATF for air transport in the country increases the cost of operation and makes it
 unviable even in areas where it has comparative advantage over other modes of transport.  The high cost of ATF has been
 adversely affecting the cost structure and profitability of our national carriers.  The issue relating to rationalization of sales tax
 on ATF has been lingering on for quite a long time.  Earlier during the course of examination of the Aircraft (Exemption from
 Taxes and Duties on Fuel and Lubricants) Bill, 2000, the Committee was informed by the Ministry of Civil Aviation in

 tax by declaring upliftment of ATF as deemed exports.  So far there has been no positive outcome of the proposal of the

58.        The above State Governments are ensuring regular passenger services to connect remote and inaccessible areas and
 district headquarters in their respective states.  Cost of deployment of helicopters is met by the State Governments out of their
 own budgets and financial assistance from the Union Government.  The Ministry of Home Affairs also utilizes helicopters for

59.        In addition to the above, Pawan Hans has provided one R-44 Robinson helicopter with M/s. Oil India Limited at

 for transportation of men and materials at their project sites since October 2000.
 
60.        During the course of the evidence of the representatives of the Ministry of Civil Aviation, the Committee observed that
 private airlines were not operating sufficient flights in the North-East region since these routes were not so profitable.  The
 Committee enquired from the representatives of Ministry of Civil Aviation about steps taken to ensure that private airlines also
 operate a reasonable number of flights to the destinations in North-East region.  In response, the Committee was informed that
 following the entry of private airlines, and their focus on lucrative trunk routes, the Government had introduced the Route
 Dispersal Guidelines with the aim of ensuring that the private domestic airlines also share the burden of connecting remote
 parts of the country. Accordingly, every scheduled private airline in the country has to follow these guidelines and undertake
 minimum prescribed flights to the specified regions in the country.  The Committee was further informed that the private
 airlines tend to follow the bare minimum of what is mandatory for them under these guidelines. 
 
61.        The Committee feels that like Indian Airlines, private airlines should also fulfil their social commitments and should not
 prefer to operate mostly on lucrative routes and complete the formality of fulfilling their social obligation by flying to the
 prescribed minimum flights to the North-East region under the Route Dispersal Guidelines.     The Committee, therefore,
 recommends that the Ministry of Civil Aviation should evolve some mechanism to ensure that private airlines in the country
 fulfil their social obligation by operating more number of flights in the North-East region.  This would help solve the problems
 of  air connectivity faced by the people of North-East region.  The Committee notices that Route Dispersal Guidelines have
 been manipulated by the private airlines to the disadvantage of the backward regions.   The Committee is, therefore, strongly of
 the view that the Route Dispersal Guidelines should be reviewed with a view to making them full proof so that no private
 airline is able to violate them and any such violation should entail heavy disincentive to that airline.
 
ADVERSE IMPACT OF THE UNION BUDGET 2004-05 ON THE CIVIL AVIATION SECTOR
 
62.        The Committee enquired from the Ministry of Civil Aviation regarding the impact of Union Budget 2004-05 on the civil
 aviation sector in the country.  In reply, the Committee was informed by the Ministry of Civil Aviation that the budget
 announcement to do away with the power to exempt the rentals for lease of aircraft and other equipment from withholding tax
 will result in additional outgo of funds from the PSUs to the lessors.   If the PSUs cannot get exemption from payment of
 withholding tax either the lessors will increase the lease rentals so as to compensate for the tax component or insist upon the
 lessee carriers to absorbing the tax component.  Both the PSUs (Indian Airlines and Air India), many existing private domestic
 scheduled operators and those who have filed applications for starting scheduled operations have to import aircraft by way of
 leasing since the purchase option takes a long time.  It is particularly so in the case of  Indian Airlines and Air India  because,
 the process of approval also has to go through various stages of examination and approval by the Government.  It is assessed
 that the additional outgo on account of lease rental could be anywhere between 10.5% to 48% of the lease cost. 
 Representations have been made to the Ministry of Finance by both the scheduled operators and the Ministry of Civil Aviation
 to restore the power to exempt withholding tax on the lease rentals.
 
63.        The Committee agrees with the view expressed by the Ministry that the provision in Union Budget 2004-2005 to do
 away with the power to exempt the rentals for lease of aircraft and other equipment from withholding tax will have an adverse
 impact on the civil aviation sector in the country particularly when the government intends to increase private sector
 participation in the provision of infrastructure facilities as well as air services.  The Committee feels that this will also have
 uneven impact on our national carriers vis-a-vis other private airlines as it would affect all other airlines which are planning
 acquisition on dry leasing.  However, the airlines, which have completed the phase of its acquisition through this route, will not
 be affected much.  The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that this power of the Ministry to exempt withholding tax
 on lease rentals should be restored.

64.        Another provision of the Union Budget 2004-05, which was brought to the notice of the Committee, was that airport
 services have been brought under the purview of service tax of 10%.  When asked about the impact of the above provision on
 the civil aviation sector, the Committee was informed that it too was likely to have an adverse impact on the civil aviation
 sector.  The Committee was informed that it was still not clear as to whether only the charges levied by the Airports would be
 subject to Service Tax or the charges of other service providers at the airports would also be subjected to Service Tax. 
 Depending upon the exact definition and description of services that are brought under Service Tax, the expenditure of all
 airlines operating to Indian airports would go up by 10.2%.  The Ministry of Civil Aviation are awaiting detailed notification
 from the Department of Revenue on this subject.
 
65.        The Committee notes that the 10
th Five-Year Plan stresses the need to have a regulatory framework in place considering
 the present size of the market, the need for monitoring quality of services and the provisions of air services for meeting social
 obligations.  However, it seems that the Government has not initiated any steps in this direction.  The Committee is of the view
 that the burden of service tax levied by the government is likely to be passed on to the users by the different airlines, which may
 be in the form of hike in passenger fares.  Presently, there is no agency to monitor as to whether the additional liability imposed
 on the airlines will be proportionately passed on to the passengers or the airlines would increase the charges at their own
 discretion in the name of levying the service tax.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that there should be some monitoring
 body to regulate the fare structure and to ensure that the fare hike passed on to the passengers due to imposition of service tax is
 just and fair.
 
66.        The Committee wanted to know from the Ministry whether the Airport Tax has been abolished by the Government and

 to furnish a detailed note on the impact of abolition of Airport Tax on the civil aviation sector.

OBSERVATIONS/CONCLUSIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS
AT A GLANCE
 
OUTLAY FOR 2004-2005 VIS-A-VIS TENTH PLAN ALLOCATION
 
According to the 10
th Five-Year Plan, the civil aviation sector has to play an important role in India's economy.  This
 sector will play a more significant role in integrating the Indian economy with the rest of the world.  But the importance
 attached to the civil aviation sector is not reflected in the outlays approved for the first two years of the 10 th Plan period of the
 Ministry of Civil Aviation.   The annual plan outlay of the Ministry of Civil Aviation was reduced from Rs.1779.18 crore for
 the year 2003-2004 to Rs.1469.77 crore at RE stage.  The reduction had been both in the Internal and Extra Budgetary
 Resources (IEBR) component as well as the Gross Budgetary support.  Now an outlay of Rs.1620.98 crore has been approved
 for the year 2004-05.  Thus an amount of Rs.3090.75 crore has been approved for the first two years of the 10
th Plan period. 
 Hence, only 23.9 per cent of the allocation has been approved for the first two years of the 10 th Plan which is fairly short of the
 proportionate 40% allocation which becomes due for this period.  The Committee recommends that keeping in view the
 importance of the civil aviation sector in the contemporary era, the Government should increase the outlay of Ministry of Civil
 Aviation and, if need be, supplement the allocation by substantially increasing the Gross Budgetary Support to the Ministry.
(Para 9)
EXPANSION OF FLEET BY INDIAN AIRLINES/AIR INDIA
 
The Committee has, during the last 3-4 years, repeatedly emphasized in its reports on Demands for Grants of the
 Ministry of Civil Aviation that there is a need for expansion of the fleet and replacement of the aged aircraft of Indian Airlines. 
 The Committee feels that the fleet acquisition programme of the national carriers i.e., both Indian Airlines and Air India, has
 been ignored for long, as a result of which the two companies have suffered both financially as well as commercially.    Delay
 in fleet acquisition forced Air India to sell the bilateral agreements to foreign airlines as a result of which Air India lost its
 market share which has gone down to 20% which was at one time at 30%. The Committee is of the opinion that atmosphere of
 uncertainty prevailed due to confusion in the Government.   The fleet acquisition programme of the two airlines could not
 materialize due to the prevailing indecisiveness with regard to the management of the companies.  Firstly, the two companies
 were placed in the list of PSUs proposed to be disinvested and then later, their names were deleted from the said list.  The
 Committee noted the fact that now the Government has decided not to go in for their disinvestment.  The Committee is of the
 view that the fleet acquisition was the basic requirement for running the two companies commercially.  The Committee,

The Committee notes that the share, which should have come from the Government, is not coming forth but only a small
 part of it has been infused as equity.  The Committee is sorry to note that there was no proposal from the Ministry for equity
 infusion in Air India and whatever efforts were made for equity infusion in Indian Airlines did not yield any result.  The

The Committee feels that high cost of ATF for air transport in the country increases the cost of operation and makes it
 unviable even in areas where it has comparative advantage over other modes of transport.  The high cost of ATF has been
 adversely affecting the cost structure and profitability of our national carriers.  The issue relating to rationalization of sales tax
 on ATF has been lingering on for quite a long time.  Earlier during the course of examination of the Aircraft (Exemption from
 Taxes and Duties on Fuel and Lubricants) Bill, 2000, the Committee was informed by the Ministry of Civil Aviation in
 November 2001 that a separate proposal was being considered to exempt Indian carriers going abroad from exemption of sales
 tax by declaring upliftment of ATF as deemed exports.  So far there has been no positive outcome of the proposal of the
 Government to exempt Indian carriers going abroad from exemption of sales tax. The Committee reiterates its recommendation
 contained in its 53
rd Report on the Bill and recommends that the proposal be implemented at the earliest.  The Committee
 further recommends that the Government should take immediate steps to exempt the Indian carriers from payment of taxes on
 ATF levied by the Central/State Governments.  The Committee strongly feels that this would certainly solve one of the long

 their cost structure and profitability.

 financial year.

The Committee recommends that IGRUA should be imparted with all possible help by the Government so that it

REPORT
           
Ministry of Tourism is the nodal authority for the formulation of national policies and programmes on Tourism and for the
 coordination of activities of various Central Government agencies, State Governments/Union Territories and the Private Sector for the
 development and promotion of tourism in the country.  The Ministry of Tourism plays a crucial role in coordinating and supplementing
 the efforts of the State/Union Territories Governments, catalyzing private investment, strengthening promotional and marketing efforts
 and in providing trained manpower resources.  The main activities of the Ministry include all policy matters, i.e. Development Policies,
 Incentives, External Assistance, Manpower Development, Promotion & Marketing and Investment Facilitation etc. Planning, Co-
ordination with other Ministries, Departments, State/ Union Territories Governments; Regulation of Standards and Guidelines;
 Infrastructure & Product Development; Human resource development through institutions and also by setting standards and guidelines;
 Publicity & Marketing; Research, Analysis, monitoring and evaluation; International Co-operation and external assistance are also
 other important functions of this Ministry.

APPROACH IN THE 10th PLAN AND ANALYSIS OF THE ANNUAL PLAN 2004-05
 
4.         The approach in the 10th Plan aims to stimulate investment and encourage the State Governments to develop unique tourism
 products. It seeks to enhance the employment potential within the tourism sector as well as to foster economic integration through
 developing linkages with other sectors.  The 10th Plan acknowledges the proven advantages of developing tourism for the promotion of
 national integration, international understanding and the earning of foreign exchange besides recognising vast employment generating
 potential of Tourism and furthering the socio-economic development. It also seeks to provide legislative and regulatory support for
 sustainable tourism and protect the interests of both the industry as well as the consumer. It further seeks to involve the rural sector in
 the promotion of all rich areas of tourism viz., rural, heritage, adventure and eco-tourism.  It focuses on the development of competitive
 high quality products and destinations besides addressing the concerns of growth through resolution of contradictions in policy so as to
 achieve inter-sectoral convergence of activities that helps to foster the growth of tourism.

EMPLOYMENT POTENTIAL WITHIN THE TOURISM SECTOR
 
10.        The Ministry of Tourism informed that the objective of annual plan 2004-05 is to enhance the employment potential within the
 tourism sector as well as to foster economic integration through developing linkages with other sectors.  The annual plan 2004-05
 focuses on the following thrust areas for sustainable growth of Tourism in the country:-
·
                       To make tourism as a major engine of economic growth;
·                       To harness the direct and multiplier effects of tourism for employment generation, economic development and
 providing impetus to rural tourism;
·                       To provide a major thrust to domestic tourism which will act as a spring board for growth and expansion of
 international tourism;
·                       To position India as a global brand to take advantage of the burgeoning global travel and trade and the vast untapped
 potential of India as a destination;
·                       To acknowledge the critical role of private sector with government working as an active facilitator and catalyst;
·                       To create and develop integrated tourism circuits based on India’s unique civilisation, heritage and culture in
 partnership with states, private sector and other agencies;
·                       To ensure that the tourist visiting India gets physically invigorated, mentally rejuvenated, culturally enriched,
 spiritually elevated and “feels India within him”;
 
11.        The Committee enquired form the Ministry of Tourism about the measures taken for effective generation of employment for
 travel & tourism sector.  The Committee was informed that India’s travel and tourism share of total employment is at 2.9 percent which
 is extremely less in comparison to other countries of the world.  There is a great potential for creating a large number of new and
 diverse jobs through expanding the frontiers of travel and tourism. The employment potential is the highest in tourism sector as
 compared to any other sectors.  The tourism industry has very strong linkages to the socio-economic progress of the country.  It has got
 a very high revenue capital ratio.  It is estimated that 1 million additional visitors could earn Rs.4300 crore of revenue for the industry. 
 It is also estimated that an investment of Rs.1 million creates 47 direct jobs and 11 indirect jobs, which far surpasses the employment
 potential from agriculture and industry sectors. 
 
 12.       During the course of oral evidence the Secretary informed that
"the Committee that the Ministry is endeavouring to position tourism as a major engine of economic growth and harness
 its direct and multiplier effect for employment generation, economic development and providing impetus to rural
 tourism.  Several schemes are being implemented to strengthen, infrastructure development, marketing and Human
 Resource Development.  These schemes will provide further impetus to generation of employment in this sector."
 
13.        The Committee notes with dismay that India's travel & tourism share of total employment is a meagre 2.9 percent which is far
 too less in comparison to other countries of the world.  This is notwithstanding the fact that employment potential of tourism sector is
 higher than Agriculture and Industrial sectors.  The Committee feels that there is an imperative need to integrate tourism with the socio-
economic objectives of the 10
th Plan so that 3.6 million jobs per year can be created through promotion of domestic and international
 tourism and thereby, India's share of international earnings from tourism can be enhanced. The Committee, therefore, recommends the
 Ministry to take proactive measures to exploit the advantages of tourism in generating employment. This is all the more important
 because tourism generates more employment in comparison to other sectors for every rupee invested.

24.        The Committee notes that the aim of product/infrastructure and destination development scheme is to improve the existing
 tourist infrastructure and create new tourist infrastructure at important tourist places of national and international importance in the
 country.  The Committee, however, notes with dissatisfaction that several new projects for development of infrastructure at identified
 destinations have been sanctioned by the Ministry of Tourism without fixing any time limit for the completion of these projects.  The
 Committee therefore, recommends the Ministry to develop competitive destinations that match international standards in terms of price,

 travellers.  The Committee also recommends that sufficient allocation to the projects should be made to avoid time and cost overruns as

 monitoring of the projects.
 
RURAL TOURISM
 
25.        The concept of Rural Tourism has been developed within the product/infrastructure and destination development scheme.  A
 provision of Rs.15 crore has been made during 2004-05 for Rural Tourism Projects.  The objective is to showcase the rural life, art,
 culture and heritage at rural locations thereby, benefit the local community economically and socially and to enable interaction between
 tourists and local population for more enriching tourist experience.
 
26.        The Ministry of Tourism informed that under the scheme, the thrust is to promote village tourism as the primary tourism
 product to spread tourism and its socio-economic benefits to rural and its new geographic regions.  Key rural areas are being identified
 for development and promotion of Rural Tourism.  The implementation is done through a Convergence Committee headed by the
 District Collector.  Activities like improving the environment, hygiene, infrastructure etc. are eligible for assistance. The software
 component i.e. training, capacity & skill building etc. is being met through the UNDP Endogenous tourism project. A maximum of
 Rs.50.00 lakh is sanctioned for each project under this scheme.  The rural tourism sites are identified with care in-consultation with
 state Govts./UT Administrations based on their potential like arts and crafts, tradition, heritage monuments, accessibility from
 established tourist centres etc.

DOMESTIC PROMOTION & PUBLICITY INCLUDING HOSPITALITY
 
42.        The potential of domestic tourism has grown substantially during the last few years due to increase in income levels and
 emergence of a dynamic urban middle class.  Domestic tourism in India is on the increase, this segment is now attaining increasing
 importance as domestic travelers have started looking at and exploring their own country with renewed interest.  Package holidays seem
 to be the order of the day as evinced by the numerous advertisements appearing in national media (Print, Electronic and Internet)
 announcing holiday packages covering a variety of themes such as adventure, eco-tours, pilgrimage etc.  Even major hotel chains are
 offering specially reduced rates during the summer months enabling those on a modest budget to avail of a unique holiday.  With higher
 disposable incomes, the domestic traveler now has a wide range of choices before him and it seems an appropriate time to tap this
 market to create tourism awareness. 
 
43.        An amount of Rs.14 crore has been allocated in B.E. 2004-05 for domestic promotion and publicity including hospitality
 regarding schemes/programmes. The Ministry informed that the existing schemes of domestic publicity, hospitality, and printing of
 literature will be merged into this scheme. The conventional publicity measures will be continued with a qualitative improvement and
 more focus on Information Technology and the electronic media.  A special focus in domestic advertising will be given to the new
 circuits being developed India’s heritage and history including the new found discoveries such as Dholavira and Cambay, the
 attractions of the North Eastern Region etc.  The domestic campaign would also envisage highlighting the new tourism circuits and
 hubs being created such as Ajanta-Allora, the Leh-Ladakh- Manali circuit, Kurukshetra, Red Fort, Hampi, Mahabalipuram, Fort of
 Rajasthan.  The Department of Tourism will continue to promote a large number of Events, fairs and festivals which have increased
 domestic tourism and have also given an impetus to international tourism.  In order to promote handicrafts in rural areas and give a
 sense of recognition to local artisans, the Ministry has been organising rural craft melas in cooperation with State Governments.  Some
 of these melas are attended even by international tourists where they can see for themselves the craftsmen at work.  Travel
 writers/Journalists/TV teams are also sponsored by the Ministry of Tourism to give better publicity to these Craft Melas.
 
44.        The Tourism Policy of the Ministry of Tourism pertaining to domestic tourism also highlights some features which are as
 under:-
·
         Creating awareness amongst all sections of society about the socio-economic benefits of tourism and about the importance of
 providing an assurance of safety and security to tourists.’
·         Promotion of eco-tourism, rural tourism and preservation of national environment and heritage.
·         Facilitating domestic tourism by promoting amenities and facilities for budget tourists.
 
45.        The Ministry informed that the figures for domestic tourist movements reflect a healthy trend.  Apart from the domestic traveler,

CO-ORDINATION BETWEEN DEPARTMENT OF TOURISM AND OTHER AGENCIES
 
53.        The travel and tourism sector is adversely affected by the lack of synergy in inter-sectoral polices.  The growth of the sector
 requires integrated and co-ordinated polices and stability in approach.  In most countries with large population, domestic tourism is the
 foundation of a viable and sustainable tourism industry. The domestic tourism market is most local or regional in nature and prefers
 recreational pursuits.  The recreation and leisure is a vital component of the quality of life particularly in urban areas. India’s physical
 infrastructure is the very foundation on which the tourism is to be built.  To achieve this goal, it is necessary to have coordination with
 various other governmental agencies viz. Ministries of Civil Aviation, Railways, Culture, and State Governments etc.
 
COORDINATION BETWEEN MINISTRY OF TOURISM AND MINISTRY OF CIVIL AVIATION
 
54.        On a question of coordination between Ministry of Tourism and Ministry of Civil Aviation, the Ministry informed the
 Committee that inter-ministerial meeting  has been convened regularly to decide the negotiating strategy for working in parallel with
 Airlines and other organizations and to improve air capacity and surface travel as well as the accommodation offer to tourists travelling
 around the country. 
 
55.        The Ministry however, informed the Committee that Air-Seat capacity on international sectors particularly during the peak
 season is inadequate. The Ministry of Tourism has received representations in this regard from the Travel Trade Associations.  The
 matter has been taken up with the Ministry of Civil Aviation for taking appropriate measures to improve the air seat capacity on
 international sectors and with the Ministry of Railways for improving connectivity to important tourist destinations. 
 
56.        During the course of evidence, the Secretary expressed that;
                                   
"there is need to increase tourism through better access and removal of barriers for growth.  There are severe
 geographical and seasonal imbalances for tourists to India during the peak period.  It is, therefore, necessary to
 introduce a system of open sky policy from the 15 top tourist generating markets during the peak season of October–
March for the next three years. Efforts are on to develop integrated Air India and Indian Airlines package tours covering
 important tourist centres in India and introducing a combined system of air and rail bookings."
 
57.        The Committee notes that Ministry of Civil Aviation and Ministry of Tourism are working in close coordination with each other
 for the growth of travel & tourism sector in the country. However, the Committee strongly feels that a restrictive air transport policy
 has a very deleterious impact on the volume of tourist traffic and recommends for a more liberal aviation regimes and a open sky policy
 for the development of tourism.

81.        The matter of rationalization of taxes on tourist transport vehicles was discussed in the 30
th meeting of Transport Development
 Council (TDC), which was held on 16th January, 2003.  The meeting was attended by the Ministers and Secretaries of the various State
 Governments.  At the meeting, the State Transport Secretaries generally expressed that the State Government do not favour any special
 dispensations to tourist transport vehicles.
 
82.        The Ministry of Tourism has pursued the matter again with the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways and it was agreed that
 the particular issue would be taken up with the States once again.  Accordingly, comments of Transport Authorities in various
 States/UTs have been called for to pursue the matter further.
 
83.        During deliberation in the meeting, the Secretary informed the Committee that;
"the present taxation structure has adverse effects on tourism industry.  This necessitates rationalization, simplification
 and uniformity in the taxation structure.  The present inter-state road taxation is a severe barrier on tourists moving
 from one State to another.  Further States have levied luxury taxes, which has had an adverse impact on tourism.  The
 high and multiplied tax structure reduces the competitiveness of the Indian Tourism Product. A consensus on uniform
 tax structure is therefore necessary."

 environment for private sector investment.  The Committee feels that the high and multiplied tax structure reduces the competitiveness
 of the Indian Tourism Products.  The Committee therefore, recommends that the Ministry of Tourism after interaction with all
 appropriate agencies should draw a package/road map and follow up the matter with the Ministry of Finance, so as to evolve uniform
 tax structure for the growth of travel & tourism sector.
